faq.q: Which files can CueSetter read?
faq.a: PDF with text, Word (.docx) and Excel (.xlsx), straight from production. You can also paste text. Scanned PDFs (images) and old .doc and .xls files can’t be read; save them as .docx or .xlsx, or paste the text.

faq.q: What if my run sheet is called something else?
faq.a: It works the same whatever the document is called: run sheet, running order, run of show, rundown, show flow, cue sheet or programme. What matters is a list of items with times or numbers, in PDF, Word, Excel or as text.

faq.q: Is my run sheet uploaded to a server?
faq.a: No. Everything is read in the browser on your own computer. The run sheet is never sent to us or any other server, so you can use it for confidential productions.

faq.q: How do I get the cue list into grandMA3?
faq.a: Download the macro as a ZIP and unzip it to the root of a USB stick. On the console, open Show Creator, choose Macros and the USB stick, import the macro and run it once. It builds the sequence with one named cue per item. If the import fails, you can paste the commands into the command line instead.

faq.q: Which grandMA3 versions does it work with?
faq.a: The macro is tested on most recent versions of grandMA3, and should in theory work on every version of grandMA3. If it doesn’t work on your version, we’d like to hear from you at hello@cuesetter.com.

faq.q: What happens to the cue numbers?
faq.a: Cue numbers follow the # in the run sheet. A set list can be split into sub-cues (12.1, 12.2) in one click, and items without a number get a number between their neighbours, for example 12.5. You can also choose running numbers 1, 2, 3.

faq.q: What does it cost?
faq.a: It’s free to try, no account needed.

excel.readsTitle: What CueSetter reads in an Excel run sheet

reads.title: Every sheet in the workbook
reads.text: One sheet per day or stage is fine. Pick the sheet you need; hidden sheets are skipped. The title above the table, or else the sheet name, becomes the sequence name.

reads.title: The header row, wherever it is
reads.text: Title and info rows at the top are skipped. The header row can be anywhere in the first 20 rows, with headers like #, Start, Time, Duration, Title or Item.

reads.title: Times as Excel shows them
reads.text: Cells formatted as time come out as 18:30, not 0.77. Repeated header rows further down are skipped.

reads.title: Items over several rows
reads.text: A row without a number or time continues the item above, so a long item or a set list stays one cue, ready to split into sub-cues.

steps.title: Upload the .xlsx file
steps.text: Drop the file into CueSetter. If the workbook has several sheets with a run sheet, choose the one for the show.

steps.title: Check the columns and cues

steps.title: Import on grandMA3
steps.text: Unzip the macro to the root of a USB stick. In Show Creator, choose Macros and the stick, import it and run it once. The sequence is built with one named cue per item.

faq.q: Can I use .xls or CSV files?
faq.a: Old .xls files can’t be read; open them in Excel and save as .xlsx. A CSV file can be opened in Excel and saved as .xlsx too, or you can copy the rows with the header and paste them into CueSetter as text.

faq.q: Is the file uploaded to a server?

template.metaTitle: Free run sheet template for Excel and Word – CueSetter
template.metaDescription: Download a free run sheet template (Excel .xlsx and Word .docx) with #, Start, Duration, Title and Notes. No sign-up. Reads straight into a grandMA3 cue list.
template.title: Free run sheet template
template.lead: A run sheet template for Excel and Word with the columns every department needs: #, Start, Duration, Title and Notes. Free, no sign-up – and it reads straight into a grandMA3 cue list.

p: One row per item, with the columns sound, lighting, video and stage management all work from:
list: # – the item number everyone calls on intercom
Start – the clock time
Duration – in minutes
Title – what happens; a set list goes on its own lines, one song per line
Notes – for sound, lighting, video and stage
after: The show’s name, date, venue, stage manager and version number go at the top. Seven example rows show how it is filled in; replace them with your show.

steps: Keep one row per item, in running order.
Give every item a number. If you add an item later, give it a number in between (12.5), so everyone’s numbers still match.
Put a set list in the title cell, one song per line under the act’s name.
Change the version number every time you send a new run sheet.
Send it as it is, or export it as PDF.

p: Lighting operators can drop the file straight into [CueSetter](/app). Every row becomes a named cue in a grandMA3 sequence, the cue numbers follow the # column, and the songs in a set list can be split into sub-cues in one click.
after: Read more about [Excel run sheets](/excel-to-grandma3) and [Word run sheets](/word-to-grandma3) in CueSetter, or [what a run sheet is](/what-is-a-run-sheet).
The same template is also on our [run of show](/run-of-show-template) and [running order](/running-order-template) pages, with tips for events and for concerts.

faq.q: Is the run sheet template free?
faq.a: Yes. Download it and use it as you like, no sign-up and no account.

faq.q: Can I use it in Google Sheets, Google Docs or Numbers?
faq.a: Yes. Open the .xlsx file in Google Sheets or Numbers, or the .docx file in Google Docs or Pages. To read it in CueSetter, download it again as .xlsx, .docx or PDF.

faq.q: Can I add or rename columns?
faq.a: Yes. Extra columns are fine. Keep the # column and a column for the title (Title, Item or Program), and CueSetter finds them by their header.

whatIs.metaTitle: What is a run sheet? Meaning, other names and what it contains – CueSetter
whatIs.metaDescription: A run sheet is the minute-by-minute plan of a show or event. What it contains, its other names (running order, run of show, rundown, cue sheet) and how it becomes a lighting cue list.
whatIs.title: What is a run sheet?
whatIs.lead: A run sheet is the minute-by-minute plan of a show or event: every item in order, with a number, start time, duration and what happens. Production writes it, and stage management, sound, lighting and video run the show from it.

p: Most run sheets are a table with one row per item. The usual columns are:
list: # – the item number, used on intercom (“standby item 12”)
Start – the clock time, often with Duration or End
Title – what happens: a speech, a song, an award, an interval
Notes per department – sound, lighting, video, stage and presenters
after: At the top there is usually the show’s name, date, venue and a version number, because the run sheet changes right up until the doors open.

sections.h: Other names for a run sheet
p: The same document has many names, depending on country and type of production:

head: Name
Where it’s used
rows: Theatre; also the music reporting form for broadcasters

after: A set list – the songs in a concert – is often part of the run sheet. A call sheet is something else: it tells the crew when to arrive.
Free templates under two of these names: [run of show template](/run-of-show-template) and [running order template](/running-order-template).

p: The run sheet is the plan for everyone. A cue list is the lighting operator’s version of it on the console: one cue for each moment the lighting changes, numbered and named so the operator can follow the stage manager’s calls.

On a grandMA3 the cue list is a sequence. Building it means typing every item from the run sheet into the console by hand – or letting [CueSetter](/) read the run sheet and make a macro that builds it.

sections.h: How to write a run sheet the lighting desk can use
list: Give every item a number, and keep the numbers when items move. Use 12.5 for an item squeezed in.
One row per item, with the start time in its own column.
Put a set list on separate lines in the title cell, so the songs can become sub-cues.
Send it as Word, Excel or a PDF exported from them – not a scanned page.
Put a version number and the date at the top.
after: Our [free run sheet template](/run-sheet-template) for Excel and Word follows these rules.

faq.q: Who writes the run sheet?
faq.a: Usually the producer or the stage manager. It is sent to everyone working on the show and updated as the plan changes.

faq.q: What is the difference between a run sheet and a cue list?
faq.a: The run sheet is the plan for the whole show. A cue list is a department’s version of it on their own equipment – for lighting, the sequence of cues on the console.

faq.q: What is the difference between a run sheet and a call sheet?
faq.a: A run sheet describes the show, item by item. A call sheet tells the crew and performers when and where to arrive.

importMacro.metaTitle: How to import a macro into grandMA3 (USB stick and onPC) – CueSetter
importMacro.metaDescription: Step by step: where to put the macro file on the USB stick, how to import it with Show Creator into the Macros pool on grandMA3 or onPC, and what to do if the import fails.
importMacro.title: How to import a macro into grandMA3
importMacro.lead: Put the macro’s XML file in grandMA3/gma3_library/datapools/macros on a USB stick, open Show Creator on the console, choose Macros and the USB stick, and import it into a free slot in the Macros pool. Then run it once.

list: A grandMA3 console, or grandMA3 onPC on a computer
The macro as an XML file
A USB stick
after: Macros made by [CueSetter](/app) come as a ZIP file with the folders already in place.

steps: Put the XML file on the USB stick in the folder grandMA3/gma3_library/datapools/macros. With a ZIP from CueSetter, unzip it to the root of the stick: the grandMA3 folder goes at the top.
Insert the stick in the console, or in the computer running onPC.
Open Show Creator from the menu (on grandMA3 1.9 it is the Import/Export menu). Choose Macros, and the USB stick as the source.
Select the macro and import it into a free slot in the Macros pool.
Run the macro by tapping it in the Macros pool.

sections.h: If the import fails: use the command line
p: A macro is a list of command lines, so the same result can be had by typing or pasting them into the command line. These are the commands a CueSetter macro uses, verified on grandMA3 onPC 2.5.1:
sections.code:
Store Sequence 101 Cue 1
Label Sequence 101 Cue 1 "Doors open"
Set Sequence 101 Cue 1 Property "Note" "Start 18:30, Duration 30"
Store Sequence 101 Cue 2
Label Sequence 101 Cue 2 "Welcome by the host"
Label Sequence 101 "Spring concert"
after: Several commands can go on one line, separated by semicolons. CueSetter shows the whole line ready to copy on the export step.

sections.h: What a macro file looks like
p: A grandMA3 macro file is XML with one MacroLine per command. DataVersion tells the console which software version the file was made for:
sections.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<GMA3 DataVersion="2.5.1.0">
  <Macro Name="Spring concert">
    <MacroLine Command="Store Sequence 101 Cue 1"/>
    <MacroLine Command="Label Sequence 101 Cue 1 "Doors open""/>
    <MacroLine Command="Label Sequence 101 "Spring concert""/>
  </Macro>
</GMA3>
after: Quotes inside a command are written as ", and the file must be saved as UTF-8.

sections.h: Make the macro from a run sheet
p: Writing a macro for a long run sheet by hand takes as long as typing the run sheet into the console. [CueSetter](/app) reads the run sheet – [PDF](/pdf-to-grandma3), [Word](/word-to-grandma3) or [Excel](/excel-to-grandma3) – and makes the macro for you, with one named cue per item and cue numbers that follow the run sheet.
Naming cues by hand instead? See [how to label cues in grandMA3](/guides/label-cues-grandma3).

faq.q: Where do I put a macro file on the USB stick?
faq.a: In grandMA3/gma3_library/datapools/macros, counted from the root of the stick. The console looks for macros in that folder.

faq.q: Can I import macros in grandMA3 onPC?
faq.a: Yes, the same way: insert the USB stick in the computer, open Show Creator, choose Macros and the stick, and import.

faq.q: The macro doesn’t show up in Show Creator. What’s wrong?
faq.a: Usually the folder: check that the file is in grandMA3/gma3_library/datapools/macros and not in an extra folder from unzipping. If it still fails, paste the commands into the command line instead.

csv.metaTitle: CSV run sheet to grandMA3 cue list – CueSetter
csv.metaDescription: How to get a CSV run sheet or cue list into grandMA3: open the CSV in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers, then save it as .xlsx or paste the rows into CueSetter. You get a macro that builds a named cue list.
csv.title: CSV run sheet to grandMA3 cue list
csv.lead: CueSetter doesn’t open .csv files directly, but a CSV is one step away. Open it in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers, then either save it as .xlsx and upload that, or copy the rows with the header and paste them into CueSetter. Either way you get a grandMA3 macro with one named cue per row.
csv.heroFrom: Rows copied from Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers

p: A CSV file is plain text: one line per row, with the cells separated by commas or semicolons. CueSetter reads Excel files and text copied from a spreadsheet, so the spreadsheet program does the CSV part:
list: Save as .xlsx: open the CSV, save or download it as an Excel workbook (.xlsx) and upload it to [CueSetter](/app). Best when you will get new versions of the file.
Copy and paste: open the CSV, select the rows including the header row, copy, and paste them into the “Or paste text” box in CueSetter. Quickest for a one-off.
after: Both give the same result: the columns are found from the header row, and every row becomes a cue.

steps: Open the CSV in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers. If everything lands in one column, use the program’s import or text-to-columns tool and choose the separator the file uses (comma or semicolon).
Check that there is a header row, with words like #, Start, Time, Duration, Title or Item.
Save it as .xlsx (in Google Sheets: File → Download → Microsoft Excel; in Numbers: File → Export To → Excel), or select the rows with the header and copy them.
Upload the .xlsx file, or paste the rows, in [CueSetter](/app). Check the columns and cues.
Download the macro and [import it on the console](/guides/import-macro-grandma3). Run it once, and the sequence is built.

sections.h: Why not paste the CSV text itself?
p: When you copy cells from a spreadsheet, they come out separated by tabs, and CueSetter reads tab-separated text with a header row column by column. The raw text of a CSV file has commas instead of tabs, so it would be read line by line, like a run sheet written as “18:30 Doors open”. That works for simple lists, but the columns are lost. Copy from the spreadsheet, not from a text editor.

sections.h: What CueSetter reads in the rows
list: The header row can be below a title or info rows; it is looked for in the first 20 rows.
Number, start time, duration and title are found from the header. Other columns, like notes, are shown but not used.
A row without a number or time continues the item above, so a set list over several rows stays one cue, ready to [split into sub-cues](/guides/sub-cues-grandma3).
Cue numbers follow the # column. Rows without a number get one between their neighbours.
after: More about spreadsheets in [Excel to grandMA3](/excel-to-grandma3). Making the run sheet from scratch? Start from the [free run sheet template](/run-sheet-template).

faq.q: Can CueSetter import a CSV file?
faq.a: Not directly. Open the CSV in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers and save it as .xlsx, or copy the rows with the header row and paste them into CueSetter as text.

faq.q: My CSV comes from a rundown or event tool. Will it work?
faq.a: If it has a header row and one row per item, yes. Open it in a spreadsheet first, check that the columns are split correctly, then save as .xlsx or copy and paste.

faq.q: Is the file uploaded to a server?
faq.a: No. Files and pasted text are read in your browser on your own computer and are never sent to us or any other server.

labelCues.metaTitle: How to name (label) cues fast in grandMA3 – CueSetter
labelCues.metaDescription: The Label command for cues and sequences in grandMA3, how to name many cues at once from the command line with semicolons, what to watch for in names, and how to label a whole cue list from a run sheet.
labelCues.title: How to name (label) cues fast in grandMA3
labelCues.lead: Use the Label command: Label Sequence 101 Cue 1 "Doors open" names cue 1, and Label Sequence 101 "Spring concert" names the sequence. To name many cues at once, put the commands on one line separated by semicolons and paste it into the command line.

p: Label gives an object a name. For a cue you give the sequence, the cue number and the name in double quotes; for the sequence itself, leave out the cue:
sections.code:
Label Sequence 101 Cue 1 "Doors open"
Label Sequence 101 Cue 2 "Welcome by the host"
Label Sequence 101 Cue 2.5 "Award"
Label Sequence 101 "Spring concert"
after: These are the same commands a CueSetter macro uses, verified on grandMA3 onPC 2.5.1. Decimal cue numbers like 2.5 work the same way; see [sub-cues and decimal cue numbers](/guides/sub-cues-grandma3).

sections.h: Name many cues in one go
p: Several commands can go on one line, separated by semicolons. Write the lines in a text editor or a spreadsheet, join them, and paste the whole line into the command line:
sections.code: Label Sequence 101 Cue 1 "Doors open"; Label Sequence 101 Cue 2 "Welcome by the host"; Label Sequence 101 Cue 3 "Fjordbyen Brass"
after: If the cues don’t exist yet, store each one before you label it: Store Sequence 101 Cue 1; Label Sequence 101 Cue 1 "Doors open". Clear the programmer first (ClearAll) so the cues are stored empty. If the cues already exist, the Label commands are enough.

sections.h: What to watch for in names
list: Double quotes end the name, so a name can’t contain them. CueSetter replaces them with an apostrophe.
Semicolons separate commands on the command line. CueSetter replaces them with a comma.
CueSetter keeps names to 40 characters and marks the ones it will shorten, so you can rewrite them before you download.
Want the time in the name? CueSetter can write “18:30 Doors open” instead of “Doors open” (Cue names: Time + title).

sections.h: Put the details in the Note field
p: A cue name should be short enough to read on the console. The rest can go in the cue’s Note property:
after: CueSetter can fill the Note field with the start time and duration, and with the rest of the title cell (a set list, details), up to 250 characters.

sections.h: Label a whole cue list from the run sheet
p: Typing 40 Label commands takes as long as typing 40 names on the console. [CueSetter](/app) reads the run sheet – [PDF](/pdf-to-grandma3), [Word](/word-to-grandma3), [Excel](/excel-to-grandma3) or [CSV via a spreadsheet](/csv-to-grandma3) – and writes the Store and Label commands for you: as a macro to [import from a USB stick](/guides/import-macro-grandma3), or as one line to paste into the command line.

faq.q: How do I rename a cue in grandMA3?
faq.a: Use Label with the sequence and cue number and the new name in double quotes, for example Label Sequence 101 Cue 3 "Main act".

faq.q: Can I name several cues at once?
faq.a: Yes. Put the Label commands on one line separated by semicolons and paste the line into the command line. CueSetter makes that line from a run sheet.

faq.q: Why are some of my cue names shortened?
faq.a: CueSetter keeps cue names to 40 characters. Names that are longer are marked in the review step, so you can shorten them yourself, and the rest of the text can go in the Note field.

subCues.metaTitle: Sub-cues and decimal cue numbers in grandMA3 – CueSetter
subCues.metaDescription: How decimal cue numbers (12.1, 12.5) work in grandMA3, how to put a cue between two others by number, and how CueSetter numbers cues from a run sheet: follow the #, split a set list into .1 .2, fill gaps with 12.5.
subCues.title: Sub-cues and decimal cue numbers in grandMA3
subCues.lead: grandMA3 cue numbers can have decimals, so 12.5 sits between cue 12 and cue 13 and 12.1, 12.2 follow straight after 12. Use them for an item added late, or for the songs in a set list, and the numbers everyone else uses stay the same.

p: On intercom the stage manager calls the run sheet’s numbers: “standby 12”. If the lighting cue for item 12 is also cue 12, nobody has to translate. When an item is squeezed in between 12 and 13, it becomes 12.5 – in the run sheet and in the sequence – and every other number stays where it was.
Sub-cues work the same way. A concert item with a set list becomes cue 12 for the act and 12.1, 12.2, 12.3 for the songs.

sections.h: Put a cue between two others
p: A cue is placed by its number, so give it a number between its neighbours:
sections.code:
Store Sequence 101 Cue 12.5
Label Sequence 101 Cue 12.5 "Award"
after: These are the commands a CueSetter macro uses for a decimal cue, verified on grandMA3 onPC 2.5.1. The cue lands between 12 and 13, and cues 13 onwards keep their numbers. To name cues quickly, see [how to label cues in grandMA3](/guides/label-cues-grandma3).

head: Run sheet
Cue numbers
rows: Item 12 with three songs, split into sub-cues
One item without a # between 28 and 29
Two items without a # between 28 and 29
One item without a # between 1 and 3

after: Gaps are filled with whole numbers when there is room, otherwise with decimals spread evenly between the neighbours, at most three decimal places. The review step tells you how many cues got an in-between number.

sections.h: Follow the run sheet, or number 1, 2, 3
list: Follow the run sheet’s # (default): the cue numbers are the item numbers, so the stage manager’s calls match the console.
Running 1, 2, 3: every item gets the next whole number, whatever the run sheet says. Sub-cues still get .1, .2.
If the # column can’t be used – missing, not a number, or not increasing – CueSetter numbers 1, 2, 3 and says so in the review.

sections.h: Split a set list into sub-cues
steps: Write the set list in the title cell of the run sheet, one song per line under the act’s name. Our [running order template](/running-order-template) is set up for that.
Upload the run sheet to [CueSetter](/app). The act becomes one cue, and the songs are kept as its note.
Press Split on that cue in the review. Each song becomes a sub-cue: 12.1, 12.2, 12.3.
Download the macro and [import it on the console](/guides/import-macro-grandma3).

faq.q: How do I insert a cue between two cues in grandMA3?
faq.a: Store it with a number between the two, for example Store Sequence 101 Cue 12.5 between cues 12 and 13. The other cues keep their numbers.

faq.q: What happens to items in my run sheet that have no number?
faq.a: With “Follow the run sheet’s #”, CueSetter gives them a number between their neighbours: a whole number when there is room, otherwise a decimal like 12.5. The rest keep their #.

faq.q: Why are my cues numbered 1, 2, 3 and not like the run sheet?
faq.a: Either Running 1, 2, 3 is chosen in the settings, or the # column couldn’t be used because numbers are missing, invalid or not increasing. The review step says which.

alternatives.metaTitle: CueSetter vs. Timecode Creator, Moving Light Assistant and Export CueList for gma3
alternatives.metaDescription: A factual comparison of CueSetter, Timecode Creator (GMA Toolbox), Moving Light Assistant and Export CueList for gma3: what each is built for, input, platform and price as stated on their own pages.
alternatives.title: CueSetter vs. Timecode Creator, Moving Light Assistant and Export CueList for gma3
alternatives.lead: They solve different problems. Timecode Creator and Export CueList for gma3 build timecoded grandMA sequences from markers in Reaper, MIDI or CSV files. Moving Light Assistant documents moving light rigs and their programming. CueSetter turns the run sheet from production – PDF, Word or Excel – into a named grandMA3 cue list, in the browser.

p: What each tool says about itself on its own pages, checked on 6 October 2026. Prices and features change; follow the sources at the bottom for the current state.

head: Tool
Built for
Input
Platform
Price, as stated
rows: Turning a run sheet into a named grandMA3 cue list
PDF with text, Word (.docx), Excel (.xlsx), pasted text
Timecoded sequences for grandMA2 and grandMA3 from markers
Reaper projects (.rpp), CSV marker files, clipboard from Excel and similar programs
Free demo mode that closes after about 10 minutes; licence at a regular price or pay what you want
Documenting moving light rigs and programming: patch, wheel loads, presets, cues with photos
List prices: Student £23.49, Personal £594.15, Institutional £1,201.22; Reader free
grandMA3 cue lists with trigger times from DAW markers, over OSC
MIDI files (Pro Tools, Logic Pro, Cubase), CSV files, Reaper projects
Mac only, macOS 12 or later (Mac App Store)
Free with in-app purchases: full version $14.99, or $1.99 a month, $2.99 for three months, $8.99 a year

p: Timecode Creator is one of the tools in GMA Toolbox by Matthias Schöffmann. Its page describes it as turning “Reaper project files or CSV marker files into timecoded sequences for grandMA consoles”: every marker becomes a cue at the marker’s time, with fade times, follow-cues and button triggers from subtracks. The result is saved as a macro and timecode for the console, or sent straight to it.
GMA Toolbox also has a Macro Generator that builds grandMA macros from a table, using templates you write yourself. It is a general tool: you decide which commands each row becomes.

Moving Light Assistant by Andrew Voller Lighting Design is documentation software: rig data, gobo and colour wheel loads, presets and cue lists with photos and notes, imported from the console. Its site lists grandMA2 among the consoles it imports from, describes grandMA3 support in version 1.4.1 as basic and improved, and says full grandMA3 support is planned for the next major release. Licences are sold through City Theatrical.

Export CueList for gma3 by OF COURSE (Maciej Hofstede) is a Mac app on the App Store. It exports cue lists from MIDI files, CSV files or Reaper projects to grandMA3 over an OSC connection, including sequence and executor numbers, trigger times and fades. Its description is written for operators who otherwise fill in every Trig Time by hand.

list: The starting point is the run sheet from production – a PDF, a Word document or an Excel file – not markers in an audio project.
You want one named cue per item, numbered like the run sheet, with set lists as sub-cues, and you will program the looks yourself.
You can’t or won’t install software: it runs in the browser on Windows, Mac or Linux, and the file is never uploaded.
You work on grandMA3. CueSetter makes grandMA3 macros, not grandMA2.
after: See it with your own file in [CueSetter](/app), or read how it handles [PDF](/pdf-to-grandma3), [Word](/word-to-grandma3) and [Excel](/excel-to-grandma3) run sheets.

list: The show runs on timecode and the cues are marked in Reaper or a DAW: Timecode Creator or Export CueList for gma3 are built for that. CueSetter makes no timecode, trigger times or fades.
You need paperwork for the rig and the programming: Moving Light Assistant.
You want macros for patch, presets or other jobs from your own command templates: GMA Toolbox’s Macro Generator.

faq.q: Is CueSetter a timecode tool?
faq.a: No. CueSetter builds a sequence with one named, empty cue per item in the run sheet. It sets no trigger times, fades or timecode.

faq.q: Does CueSetter work with grandMA2?
faq.a: No. The macro is made for grandMA3 and tested on most recent grandMA3 versions.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: No. CueSetter runs in the browser, and the run sheet is read on your own computer, never uploaded.

runOfShow.metaTitle: Free run of show template (Excel and Word) – CueSetter
runOfShow.metaDescription: Download a free run of show (ROS) template for events and conferences, in Excel .xlsx and Word .docx: #, Start, Duration, Title and Notes. No sign-up, and ready to become a grandMA3 cue list.
runOfShow.title: Free run of show template
runOfShow.lead: A run of show (ROS) template for corporate events, conferences and galas, in Excel and Word. One row per segment with number, start time, duration, title and notes for every department. Free, no sign-up, and ready for the lighting desk.

sections.h: What a run of show needs
p: A run of show is the schedule the whole crew calls the event from. Ours has the columns that matter on show day:
list: # – the segment number the show caller uses
Start – the clock time the segment begins
Duration – in minutes, so overruns are easy to spot
Title – the segment: walk-in, opening video, keynote, panel, award, break
Notes – mics, playback, lighting, stage changes
after: The file is called run-sheet-template: run of show, run sheet and running order are the same document with different names. See [what a run sheet is](/what-is-a-run-sheet) for the full list.

sections.h: Tips for an event or conference
steps: Give every segment a number, including walk-in, breaks and walk-out. They are moments the lighting changes too.
Put each speaker or award on its own row, so each gets its own cue.
When a segment is added late, number it between its neighbours (4.5) instead of renumbering the rest.
Change the version number at the top every time you send it out, and say what changed.
Send it as Excel, Word or a PDF exported from them – not a scan.

sections.h: From run of show to lighting cues
p: The lighting operator can drop the file into [CueSetter](/app) and get a grandMA3 macro that builds one named cue per segment, numbered like the run of show. It works the same with a run of show you didn’t make from this template, as long as it is a [PDF](/pdf-to-grandma3), [Word](/word-to-grandma3) or [Excel](/excel-to-grandma3) file.
after: Working on a concert or a TV show instead? The [running order template](/running-order-template) explains set lists and sub-cues.

faq.q: What is a run of show?
faq.a: The minute-by-minute schedule of an event: every segment in order, with start time, duration and what happens. In the US it is the usual name for what the UK calls a run sheet or running order.

faq.q: What should a run of show include?
faq.a: At least a number, start time, duration and title for every segment, plus notes for the departments that act on it. Put the event name, date, venue and a version number at the top.

faq.q: Is the run of show template free?
faq.a: Yes. Download the Excel or Word file and use it as you like, with no sign-up and no account.

runningOrder.metaTitle: Free running order template for concerts and events (Excel, Word) – CueSetter
runningOrder.metaDescription: Download a free running order template in Excel .xlsx and Word .docx, with room for set lists. #, Start, Duration, Title and Notes. No sign-up. In CueSetter, each set list becomes grandMA3 sub-cues.
runningOrder.title: Free running order template
runningOrder.lead: A running order template for concerts, festivals and live TV, in Excel and Word. Each act or item gets a row with number, start time, duration and title, and the set list goes in the same cell, one song per line. Free, no sign-up.

p: In a concert running order the songs matter as much as the acts. The template keeps both together:
list: One row per act or item, with # for the number called on intercom
Start and duration, so changeovers and curfew are visible
The act’s name on the first line of the title cell, and its songs on the lines below
Notes for sound, lighting, video and stage
after: The file is called run-sheet-template; in the UK the same document is often called the running order. More names in [what a run sheet is](/what-is-a-run-sheet).

sections.h: How to write a running order the crew can follow
steps: Number every item, including changeovers and the interval.
Write the songs under the act, one per line, in the order they are played.
When an item is added, give it a number between its neighbours (6.5), so the numbers on everyone’s paper still match.
Put the show, date, venue and a version number at the top, and change the version every time.
Send the Excel or Word file, or a PDF exported from it.

p: Upload the running order to [CueSetter](/app): every item becomes a named cue in a grandMA3 sequence, numbered like the running order. Press Split on an act and each song becomes a sub-cue – 6.1, 6.2, 6.3. [Sub-cues and decimal cue numbers](/guides/sub-cues-grandma3) explains the numbering.
after: Planning a conference or corporate event? The [run of show template](/run-of-show-template) has tips for segments and speakers.

faq.q: What is a running order?
faq.a: The order of a show, item by item, with times: acts, songs, speeches and changeovers. It is the usual UK name for a run sheet, especially in concerts and TV.

faq.q: What is the difference between a running order and a set list?
faq.a: A set list is the songs one act plays. A running order is the whole show, and often includes each act’s set list.

faq.q: Is the running order template free?
faq.a: Yes. Download the Excel or Word file and use it as you like, with no sign-up and no account.
